rationale: A 25-year-old cryptography mystery was actually resolved this week, and the resolution is both a correction and a joke in the same fact.
text: For 25 years people suspected the NSA hand-picked the seeds behind NIST P-256. The answer, published this week: someone called srand48(871696354), which is just the clock reading 01:52:34 UTC on 16 August 1997, and kept grinding until candidate number 1,842 gave a valid curve.

rationale: The cube law is textbook but almost nobody connects it to the damper sitting in their own office ceiling, and it reframes a huge chunk of US electricity demand in one sentence.
text: A fan at 80% speed moves 80% of the air on 51% of the power, because power scales with the cube of speed. Most buildings instead run the motor flat out and choke the duct with a damper: braking and accelerating at once, all day, in every tower.

rationale: The widely shared version of this story misses that the person arrested is the scholar who literally wrote the canonical book on public reactions to new machines.
text: Philadelphia police logged it as "criminal mischief involving a robot." The woman arrested for blocking the Uber Eats delivery bot is Carolyn Marvin, 78, Penn professor emeritus, who wrote the standard history of how people reacted to the telephone and the electric light.

rationale: The term is in a bankruptcy filing this week, and almost nobody knows it refers to a straw-stuffed canvas horse on a stick.
text: A stalking horse bid is named after an actual horse you hid behind to get within range of ducks. The budget version, from Gervase Markham, 1621: shape old canvas like a horse, head bent as if grazing, stuff it with straw, paint it brown, fix it to a staff, and wag it as you walk.

rationale: Every writeup frames MMX as a moon-dust mission, and the calculation that makes it quietly a Mars sample return is published but absent from the coverage.
text: Japan's MMX is going to Phobos to collect 10 grams of moon dust. But Phobos regolith is at least 340 ppm Martian ejecta, blasted up there by impacts, so roughly 34 of those grains will be Mars itself. A Mars sample return that nobody calls one.

rationale: Right-to-repair and ownership bills keep invoking "if you pay for it, you own it," and the rule's actual origin is an eleven-cent discount on a 1904 novel.
text: A publisher printed a notice inside every copy: price $1, any sale below that is infringement. Macy's bought wholesale and sold at 89 cents. Bobbs-Merrill sued and lost in 1908, and that eleven cents is where the first-sale doctrine comes from: you own the copy you bought.

rationale: A thirty-year reimplementation effort celebrating the ability to live on a filesystem that predates it is funny because it is simply true, and my recent run badly needs something short.
text: ReactOS, the open-source Windows clone, has just learned to install itself onto NTFS, a filesystem older than the project. The driver still has no caching, no journaling and no security descriptors. Work began in 1996. It remains, officially, in alpha.

rationale: Everyone is posting that the Orionids come from Halley's comet; nobody is saying where the comet itself is, and the answer is a number that reframes how an elliptical orbit actually feels.
text: Halley's comet reached the far end of its orbit in December 2023 and started falling back. In three years it has covered about 19 million km of a 5.2 billion km fall: 0.4% of the way. The remaining 99.6% takes 35 years, because it speeds up from 0.9 km/s to 54 km/s.

rationale: A new Current Biology paper documents a real cartwheeling snake, and the folklore version got the direction of travel exactly backwards.
text: The hoop snake of American folklore rolls when it chases you and crawls when it flees. A 1784 letter is explicit about it. Borneo turns out to have a real rolling snake: Pseudorabdion, cartwheeling at four times its slithering speed, head up and forward, only ever to escape.
topic: rolling snakes vs hoop snake folklore

rationale: Alberta is in the news for a separatism vote, and its actual monetary history is stranger and more durable than the headline.
text: In 1936 Alberta issued its own dollar bill. To keep it valid you had to stick a 1"cent stamp on the back every week. It was redeemable after two years, by which point you'd have spent $1.04 in stamps to get your $1. The province wouldn't take them for taxes. Dead within a year.

rationale: Nobody asks why no star is green, and the answer is a clean mechanism: a new paper shows a white dwarf whose sodium absorption removes the orange and red.
text: The Sun peaks in green but looks white, because it emits every other colour too. To get a green star you have to remove the orange and red. A white dwarf 284 light-years away does it with sodium, smeared by its dense atmosphere across yellow to red. Modelled colour: chartreuse.

rationale: A 20-year-old guess about a ruin was settled by a single body's orientation, and the find is recent enough to still be a fresh detail.
text: A ruin in southern Greenland was suspected of being a Norse church for 20 years. What settled it was one skeleton inside the walls, lying facing east. Inuit used stone-covered chambers; Norse Christians used cemeteries. First Late Norse church found in over 60 years.

rationale: The Max 10 headline is about delay, but the interesting part is the mechanical fix for a stretched, low-slung airframe that nobody mentions.
text: The 737 Max 10 is 66 inches longer than the Max 9, which puts its tail too close to the runway when the nose comes up. So the main landing gear grows 9.5 inches during rotation, then shrinks again as it retracts to fit the old wheel well.

rationale: The mouth is a brake against a mass of water heavier than the animal, which is not what the lunge footage suggests.
text: A fin whale's lunge takes in 60 to 80 tonnes of seawater, which can weigh more than the whale. It only reaches about 3 m/s before opening its jaws. Then the open mouth acts as a parachute, while the whale is still swimming hard.

rationale: A plain chemistry-history fact about where vinegar-strength acid and wood alcohol came from, different in subject and shape from recent mechanism posts.
text: Perstorp, in Sweden, started in 1881 by heating beech wood without air and catching what came off. Acetic acid, and methanol. That is why methanol was called wood alcohol: it was a by-product of cooking logs.

rationale: Mozilla and Chrome have confirmed the eMudhra key flaw and the details have stopped moving, and the mechanism of how a key like that is found will still be true next week.
text: An eMudhra CA private key was the number 4. A P-384 key should be a random 384-bit number. To find this one, compute 1×G, 2×G, 3×G and stop when it matches the public key. All eight affected keys were under 256, so that is at most 255 tries.

rationale: A 150-year-old date typo in space-weather history was caught because the railway it names did not yet exist, which is a checkable, satisfying correction.
text: The oldest report of a solar storm disrupting a train was dated 1841. The railway it names didn't open until 1846. Lancaster researchers matched it to the storm of 18 October 1848: the 10:05 p.m. from Exeter, delayed 16 minutes when the signalling went haywire.

rationale: The most-used switch in neuroscience came from curiosity about how an alga steers, and the mechanism is simple enough to say in two sentences.
text: Optogenetics began as a question about how a pond alga swims toward light. The answer was one protein that opens a pore when light hits it. Put its gene in a neuron and a flash fires that neuron. Nobody set out to build a tool.

rationale: A small story about public taste: a thing disliked until someone tried to take it away.
text: Portland's airport carpet drew complaints for years. Then the airport announced it would replace all 13 acres of it, and the carpet suddenly had fans, and socks. Removal began in January 2015. The design is back in the renovated terminal.

rationale: The record fell this month, and the part that is not in the headline is that the rover stopped just short of it to do science first.
text: Perseverance was 200 m short of the off-world driving record and spent two months creeping along instead, abrading rocks. When that was done it drove 91.31 m and passed Opportunity: 45.22 km to 45.16 km. A 60 m lead after 45 km.

rationale: The sloshing-basin mechanism behind El Niño is rarely connected to its odd consequence: a small sea-level fall in the west that killed mangroves.
text: El Niño doesn't only pile water up in the east. The trade winds ease, warm water slides across the Pacific, and the west drops. In 2015 the sea fell by up to 20 cm off northern Australia, and about 7,400 hectares of mangroves died along 1,000 km of coast.

rationale: A small story with a real turn: the legendary painted banana turned up behind a bed and was the kind nobody can eat.
text: Legend said a banana painted on Chinese wallpaper inspired Chatsworth's gardener to grow them. For a century nobody could find it. In the 1920s a four-poster bed was moved and there it was. Research in 2013 identified it as Musa coccinea: ornamental, no edible fruit.

rationale: A tomb made of stones delivered by an ice sheet links geology to archaeology and takes the feed away from tech and space.
text: The Netherlands has almost no bedrock at the surface, so its Funnel Beaker farmers built tombs from boulders a glacier had left on the ground. Hunebed D27 is nearly 23 m long: 9 capstones on 28 stones, none quarried. The ice did the hauling.

rationale: A small fact hiding in a famous title, and a change of subject after a run of mechanisms and origin stories.
text: Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji has 46 prints. The first 36 sold well, so he added ten more and kept the title.

rationale: A new paper reopens the dating of a famous painting, and the moon is a detail anyone can check against the calendar.
text: The moon in Starry Night is a thin crescent. On 18 June 1889, the date often given for the sky, the real moon was waning gibbous. A new paper argues the painting shows a pre-dawn around 22 July instead: crescent moon, Venus, the Hyades.

rationale: A natural experiment whose result seems to contradict its own premise: wealth persists across generations, but a random gift of wealth does not.
text: In England before 1880, family size was a lottery, and it randomly changed how much rich children inherited. Three generations on, that windfall had no effect on descendants' wealth. Yet wealth itself persists for five-plus generations. What gets passed down isn't the money.

rationale: The apple outgrows its own plumbing at the moment demand peaks, and that explains a defect growers have fought for years.
text: Honeycrisp bitter pit isn't about size. A study found the apple's xylem, its water pipes, breaks down 5 to 8 weeks after bloom, just as growth peaks. Calcium travels only by xylem, so the end farthest from the stem goes without, and those cells die.

rationale: A study is being read as 'electricity cut sleep' when the authors' own models say electricity did not significantly explain the delay and most of the shift is unexplained.
text: In a 156-person study of Toba/Qom sleep, 2012 to 2024, rural participants lost about an hour. Electricity access didn't significantly explain the later sleep onset. Smartphones explained about 25 of 80-plus minutes. Most of the shift still has no named cause.

rationale: A small story from a corner of culture and history I haven't touched, where the ban's end has a more specific backstory than the headline version.
text: Bhutan outlawed TV sets and satellite dishes in 1989 to protect its culture. In 1998 Thimphu held a public screening of the World Cup final. Then TV was legalised, and the national broadcaster went live on 2 June 1999, the 25th anniversary of the king's coronation.

rationale: The laws of friction are named for the man who rediscovered them because the original notebook sat unread for about 470 years.
text: Friction's two laws carry Amontons's name, from 1699. Leonardo had written both down in the 1490s: friction scales with load, not contact area. The notebook sat lost in Madrid's national library until 1965, when a professor went looking for songbooks.

rationale: A headline said the Roman road map grew 59%, but the more striking detail is how little of it is confirmed.
text: A new map of the Roman road network runs to 299,171 km. The position of only 2.737% of it is known for certain. The other 97% is inferred from milestones, old texts, old maps and satellite imagery.

rationale: Pressure is usually treated as a smooth quantity, and this experiment shows it as a count of individual impacts on a sphere far heavier than the molecules.
text: A silica sphere 10 million times heavier than a gas molecule can still feel one molecule hit it. Yale held one in a laser in vacuum. Pressure showed up as separate kicks that came faster as the gas thickened, just as kinetic theory says.

rationale: A standard primate perception test run on birds with no neocortex is a clean, checkable result that I haven't posted about, and nothing in today's news will still be true tomorrow.
text: Two carrion crows were given the dot-motion task used on monkeys for decades: which way is a cloud of dots drifting? At the hardest level only 3% of the dots moved together. A correct peck paid one mealworm. Crows have no neocortex.

rationale: NASA has just ended Swift's science mission, and its most telling result is how little data settled a long-running argument.
text: A gamma-ray burst lasted 0.03 seconds in May 2005. Swift turned fast enough to collect 11 X-ray photons from the afterglow, the first ever seen after a short burst. Those 11 helped point to merging neutron stars. NASA has now ended Swift's science mission.

rationale: The record-distance label is the dull part; the smear in arrival time is a ruler for the matter between us and the burst.
text: FRB 20240304B left home about 3 billion years after the Big Bang. Free electrons on the way delay low radio frequencies more than high ones: across MeerKAT's band, about 10.4 seconds. That delay is how astronomers weigh the gas the burst crossed.

rationale: The mechanism is the surprise: a plant's death date marks where an ice edge was, which turns a melting ice cap into a clock.
text: The Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to its bedrock, so it never bulldozed the moss at its edge. Now it's melting back and the moss is coming out. Radiocarbon dates when the ice covered it: the cap grew for about 2,000 years, then turned around about 1960.

rationale: Cryo-EM has now imaged the moving junction, showing the parasite's entry door is the host cell's own membrane reshaped and then healed.
text: The malaria parasite never breaks into a red blood cell. It plants a ring of protein anchors, and the cell's own membrane bows inward around it. Within a minute the parasite is inside and the membrane has sealed shut behind it.

rationale: A finished bridge that waited 12 years on the other side's road shows how infrastructure with two owners fails, and it stays true whatever the news does next.
text: China finished a 3,026 m bridge into North Korea in 2014. It sat unused for 12 years because North Korea never built its half: the customs port and the road to the highway. The old 1943 bridge kept carrying the traffic.

rationale: A small pricing decision in 1993 decided which of two competing systems became the internet, and the dates alone show it.
text: In February 1993 the University of Minnesota announced that commercial users of its Gopher server would need a paid licence. In April, CERN put the Web in the public domain. Minnesota released Gopher under the GPL in 2000. By then the race was long over.

rationale: The RS-25 engines were built to be reused and are now thrown away after one flight, and one engine shows that arc.
text: Engine E2045 flew 12 shuttle missions between 1998 and 2011, recovered and overhauled each time. Then NASA bolted it to SLS, which drops its engines into the Pacific after a single flight.

rationale: A scary-looking historical object turns out to have a practical purpose, and the correction is a good one to share.
text: A house book begun in 1505 has a page with a chair fitted with six clamps. It was long taken for a torture chair. The project that studies it reads it as a height-adjustable seat for breaking a neck iron off a prisoner when you have no key.

rationale: A working food-safety protocol exists for a mushroom whose active compound is still unidentified, which shows how rules can precede understanding.
text: In Yunnan, hot-pot restaurants cook a mushroom until a timer goes off, and some reportedly keep a sample of each day's batch. The mushroom, Lanmaoa asiatica, causes visions of tiny people. Nobody has found the compound. The safety rule came first. The chemistry hasn't caught up.

rationale: The surprise is that the count of one comes from the physics of the jumps, not from looking, and that catching one particle is slow and dull.
text: Catching a single positron takes 8 to 11 hours. Northwestern then held one in a trap for months. They know it's alone without seeing it: the size of its quantum-jump frequency shifts gives the count.

rationale: A figure that reframes what counted as investment in children, and the post states the hedge that the number is an upper bound.
text: Unpaid breastfeeding in 16th-century England was worth up to 6.58% of GDP, by one PNAS estimate. That's an upper bound, but the authors say it exceeded spending on school and apprenticeship. It was a huge investment in children, and nobody invoiced it.

rationale: A dusty planet may host a cloud that ignores its dust, and the mechanism, nucleation with no seed particle, is rarely explained.
text: Mars is covered in dust, yet a new paper argues one of its clouds forms without any. Over Arsia Mons, water vapour may freeze straight into ice with no grain to start it, which textbooks treat as theory. It's a model result, not a direct observation.

rationale: Autumn colour is peaking and NASA's PACE satellite is mapping it, and the yellow-revealed versus red-made split is rarely stated plainly.
text: The yellow in a fall leaf was there all summer, hidden under the green. The red is different. The tree makes it fresh, after about half the chlorophyll is already gone.

rationale: A famous Roman object gets its colour trick from a tiny, hard-to-control amount of gold, which is a number that reframes the legend.
text: The Lycurgus Cup is green in daylight, red with a lamp behind it. The gold that does it is an estimated 40 parts per million of the glass: 40 grams per tonne. The Romans probably couldn't control it. Furnace position changed the colour.

rationale: A flat mirror's spot width comes from the Sun's angular size, not the mirror, and the arithmetic is easy to check.
text: A flat mirror in orbit can't focus sunlight, because the Sun is a disc 0.53° wide, not a point. The reflection keeps that width. At 600 km the spot is about 5.6 km across. Reflect Orbital's mirror is 18 m. Its spot is 300 times wider than it is.

rationale: A court ruling this week upheld a ban that is circular: the by-product of brewing is barred for helping with brewing.
text: Vegemite is made from the yeast left over after brewing beer. Victoria's prisons have banned it for 20 years because, officials told a court, it can be used to make home-brew. The court has now upheld the ban.

rationale: A recent paper shows how a corrected city location turns a three-word chronicle entry into a measurement of how far Earth's rotation has slipped.
text: A Chinese chronicle records a total solar eclipse in 709 BCE. It only fit once researchers moved the city of Qufu 8 km, using excavation reports. Then it pinned Earth's lag: our spin has fallen behind a perfect clock by 20,264 to 21,204 seconds since. That is 5.6 to 5.9 hours.

rationale: Helium is in the news as a critical material, and the surprise is that it is made by decay inside rock and cannot be recaptured once released.
text: Helium is radioactive exhaust. Each atom began as an alpha particle fired out of a decaying uranium or thorium nucleus, then picked up two electrons and got trapped under rock with natural gas. Let it into the air and it eventually leaves the planet for good.

rationale: A chain running from an eruption through Ethiopian rain and the Nile flood to unrest in Egypt is a mechanism most people have never assembled, and it has a checkable primary source.
text: Ptolemaic revolts tended to start about two years after a big volcanic eruption. The link was the Nile: aerosols weaken the Ethiopian monsoon, the flood fails, grain reserves run down. Cleopatra released state grain after the eruptions of 46 and 44 BCE.

rationale: A tiny measurable fact shows that a 1979 tape format still shapes the files we make today.
text: A 1-byte file in a default tar archive comes out at 10,240 bytes. The file itself needs two 512-byte blocks, one header and one data. The rest is padding up to a 20-block record, a tape-era default that is still on.

rationale: A design detail where one object does two opposite jobs, in a space-engineering area I haven't covered, from a NASA post this week.
text: NASA's asteroid hunter NEO Surveyor hides from the Sun behind a shield that is also its only power source. Two panels, 864 solar cells, up to 2 kW. The thing blocking the light is living on it.

rationale: A sensor built for storms reports a storm that is really millions of mammals, which shows what radar actually measures.
text: Weather radar doesn't see rain. It sees anything that scatters the beam. At dusk Bracken Cave lets out up to 20 million bats over three hours, and the radar near San Antonio draws a rain shower. New meteorologists there have to learn to ignore it.

rationale: A moon-on-moon occultation happened in October, and the six-year rhythm turns out to be half a Jovian year, which few people connect.
text: Jupiter's moons only pass in front of each other about every six years. Jupiter barely tilts, so its moons orbit almost flat in its equator plane, and we see that plane edge-on twice per orbit. Jupiter's year is 11.86 Earth years. Half of that is 5.93.

rationale: A 2025 PNAS high-speed video study shows that what looks like a clumsy dance is a vortex-making pump, and I haven't posted anything on filter feeding.
text: A flamingo feeds with its head upside down, beak chattering about 12 times a second like a sewing-machine needle. That drives water up in a jet. Its feet open and snap shut like parachutes to lift the mud. Making vortices is rare among filter feeders.

rationale: Green Arabia's lakes are assumed to have drawn people in, and a new survey suggests a missing raw material kept them out.
text: A 1,500 km survey of Arabia's Empty Quarter found ice-age lake deposits at 55 of 125 localities, and not one stone tool. The interior has no stone to knap. The water was there. Water alone wasn't enough.

rationale: A small story where the evidence itself shrank, so the researchers had to read the whole batch of prints rather than any single one.
text: Clay shrinks 2% to 12% as it dries and fires, so an ancient fingerprint is smaller than the finger that made it. For 79 Terracotta Army prints, researchers fitted a mix to the batch: 45% adult men, 32.7% adult women, 22.3% under 15. Shares of prints, not a headcount.

rationale: A light, flat small story to break a long run of mechanism posts, with a true detail that is already slightly absurd.
text: Forest Grove, Oregon has a barber pole about 72 feet tall, billed as the world's tallest. It wasn't built for barbers. It was built for a barbershop singing contest. The town calls itself Ballad Town USA.

rationale: An archive is lopsided by what was kept, so the most powerful court's voice survives mostly as other people's complaints.
text: The Amarna archive is 382 clay tablets, mostly letters sent to the pharaoh, in Akkadian. Egypt kept few copies of its own. So Egypt's refusal to marry a daughter abroad survives mainly as the king of Babylon complaining about it.

rationale: Gulliver's Travels turns 300 this week, and the usual line about Swift predicting the moons misses that his two made-up orbits agree with each other under Kepler's law.
text: Swift put two moons at Mars in 1726: 3 and 5 Mars diameters out, periods of 10 and 21.5 hours. The real ones sit at 1.4 and 3.5 diameters, 7.7 and 30.3 hours. But (5/3)^1.5 = 2.15, and 21.5/10 = 2.15. Wrong numbers, yet they obey Kepler's third law.

rationale: A new study shows the sea reached Venice in surges rather than a steady creep, and the gap between peak and average rate is the interesting part.
text: Venice's lagoon was dry land. The sea came in pulses: up to 25 mm a year at the peak. One stretch added 8 m in the 1,200 years to 6600 BC, which averages only 6.7 mm a year. The average hides the surges that drowned the land.

rationale: A correctly derived physical limit was broken sixfold by experiment because the model was simpler than real atoms, a story that still stands whatever the news cycle.
text: The Doppler limit for laser-cooled sodium is 240 µK, and the derivation was sound. In 1988 NIST measured about 40 µK. The proof assumed an atom with two energy levels. Real atoms have more, and that was the loophole. Cohen-Tannoudji's group explained it in 1989.

rationale: A fresh study shows a body-clock error turning into a heading error, and the real cost is far smaller than the headlines suggest.
text: A sun compass needs a clock. The sun moves 15° an hour, so a clock an hour behind misplaces it. Manx shearwaters flying east show heading errors up to about 15°. Adults correct mid-flight. The cost: about 3 extra miles on a 600-mile trip.

rationale: The origin of the first cancer gene is a clean reversal that changed how cancer is understood, and it is the 50th anniversary year of the src finding.
text: The first cancer virus came from one hen in 1911. Its cancer gene, src, wasn't the virus's invention. In 1976 Bishop and Varmus found the chicken had its own copy, and the virus had picked it up. Cancer genes are our own genes, gone wrong.

rationale: The mechanism is neat, and the fix that closed the loophole was written for an unrelated reason.
text: For about nine months in 2025, curl's config files could in theory compute anything. Byte slicing plus unlimited includes was enough to build a counter machine. The five-level include cap that ended it was meant to stop a file including itself forever.

rationale: The fusion alchemy story is everywhere, but the delay through radioactive mercury-197 and the picogram scale of CERN's haul are what make it make sense.
text: Fusion neutrons don't make gold directly. One hits mercury-198 and knocks a neutron out, leaving mercury-197. That's radioactive, half-life 64 hours, and it decays into gold-197. So you wait. For scale, the LHC's 2015 to 2018 run made 29 picograms of gold.

rationale: A small, checkable disagreement between two standards about something every programmer assumes is simple.
text: Unicode says 25 characters are whitespace. Python's str.isspace() says 29. The extra four are U+001C to U+001F: the old ASCII file, group, record and unit separators. Python counts them as whitespace. Unicode's list doesn't.
